name: Greek Pantheon
culture: Ancient Greek
description: The Greek pantheon encompasses the gods and goddesses of ancient Greek mythology, centered on Mount Olympus and featuring the twelve Olympians who ruled after the Titanomachy.
detailedHistory:
## Origins of the Olympians

The Greek pantheon emerged from the mingling of indigenous Pelasgian beliefs with the sky-god traditions of invading Hellenic tribes.

### The Golden Age

Before the gods, there were the Titans, ruled by Cronus. This was a time of peace and prosperity, but also stagnation. The rise of Zeus and the Olympians marked the beginning of a new cosmic order—civilization, law, and justice replacing the raw elemental forces of the Titans.

### Mount Olympus

The twelve major gods (Olympians) dwelt on Mount Olympus, the highest peak in Greece. From their divine palaces, they observed human affairs, intervening to reward piety or punish hubris.

name: Norse Pantheon
culture: Norse/Germanic
description: The Norse pantheon includes the Aesir and Vanir gods of Scandinavian mythology, centered in Asgard and featuring stories of creation, heroism, and the prophesied end of the world known as Ragnarok.
detailedHistory:
## Late sources for an older religion

Almost everything told about the Norse gods comes from Iceland in the 13th century, two hundred years after the island's conversion to Christianity around 1000 CE. The *Poetic Edda*, a collection of anonymous mythological and heroic poems preserved mainly in the Codex Regius (c. 1270), includes *Völuspá*, the seeress's account of the world from creation to Ragnarök, and *Hávamál*, the sayings of Odin. Some of these poems are probably much older than the manuscript. Snorri Sturluson's *Prose Edda* (c. 1220) is a handbook for poets that retells the myths in systematic prose; it is the source of many familiar details, but Snorri was a Christian scholar organising inherited material, and scholars read him with care.

## Other witnesses

Older and independent evidence is patchier: skaldic poems composed for Viking-age rulers and quoted in the sagas, runic inscriptions, picture stones on Gotland, carvings such as the Thor fishing stones at Altuna and Gosforth, place names across Scandinavia that preserve the names of Thor, Odin, Frey, and Ullr, Adam of Bremen's description (c. 1075) of a temple at Uppsala with images of Thor, Wodan, and Fricco, and, much earlier, Tacitus's *Germania* (98 CE) on the religion of the continental Germanic peoples. Saxo Grammaticus's Latin *Gesta Danorum* (c. 1200) retells some of the same figures as ancient kings.

## Æsir and Vanir

The sources describe two groups of gods, the Æsir (Odin, Thor, Frigg, Týr, Baldr, and others) and the Vanir (Njörðr, Freyr, Freyja), associated with fertility, wealth, and the sea. They fought a war that ended in a truce and an exchange of hostages, after which the Vanir lived among the Æsir. Whether that war reflects a historical merging of cults is an old scholarly question with no settled answer.

## The world and its end

The cosmos is organised around the ash Yggdrasil and its nine worlds. *Völuspá* tells how the gods order the world from the body of the giant Ymir, how Baldr is killed, and how Ragnarök, the doom of the gods, will bring Fenrir, the Midgard Serpent, Surtr's fire, and the deaths of Odin and Thor, before a green earth rises again from the sea. How much of that ending reflects Christian influence is debated. Religious practice itself, blót sacrifice, feasting, and oath-taking, is known mainly from saga descriptions written long after.

name: Egyptian Pantheon
culture: Ancient Egyptian
description: The Egyptian pantheon encompasses the gods and goddesses of ancient Egypt, featuring creation deities, solar worship, the afterlife, and the eternal struggle between order (Ma'at) and chaos (Isfet).
detailedHistory:
## Three thousand years of religion

Egyptian religion was practised from before the unification of the country (c. 3100 BCE) until the closing of the last temples in late antiquity; the temple of Isis at Philae functioned until the 6th century CE. Over that span gods rose and fell in importance, merged (Amun-Ra, Ra-Horakhty), and were worshipped differently in different cities. There was no single creed or scripture: each major temple had its own theology, and several creation accounts coexisted without contradiction being a problem.

## Creation accounts

At Heliopolis, Atum emerges on the primeval mound from the waters of Nun and produces Shu and Tefnut, from whom come Geb and Nut and their children Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys, the Ennead. At Hermopolis, eight primordial beings, the Ogdoad, precede the sun. At Memphis, the *Shabaka Stone* (c. 710 BCE, copying an older text) presents Ptah creating through heart and tongue, thought and word.

## The written sources

The *Pyramid Texts*, carved inside royal pyramids at Saqqara from the reign of Unas (c. 2350 BCE), are the oldest religious texts. They were adapted for non-royal burials in the *Coffin Texts* of the Middle Kingdom and, from the New Kingdom, in the *Book of the Dead*, illustrated papyri of spells to guide the deceased. Underworld books such as the *Amduat* and the *Book of Gates* map the sun's night journey on royal tomb walls in the Valley of the Kings. Egyptian texts rarely tell myths as continuous narratives; the fullest account of the Osiris story is in Greek, in Plutarch's *On Isis and Osiris* (c. 100 CE), alongside Egyptian allusions and the New Kingdom tale *The Contendings of Horus and Set*.

## Maat and the afterlife

Maat, truth and right order, was what king and temple ritual existed to uphold against isfet, disorder. The dead hoped to be judged justified before Osiris, their heart weighed against Maat's feather (Book of the Dead Spell 125), and to live on in the Field of Reeds or travel with the sun. Temples were the houses of the gods, served daily by priests on the king's behalf, and ordinary people approached the gods through festivals, household cults, amulets, and oracles.

name: Roman Pantheon
culture: Ancient Roman
description: The Roman pantheon adapted Greek mythology while emphasizing duty, piety, and state religion. Romans identified their gods with Greek counterparts but maintained distinct rituals, festivals, and a practical approach to divine favor.
detailedHistory:
## Religion as practice

Roman religion was above all a matter of correct practice: sacrifice, vows, festivals, and the reading of signs, carried out by magistrates and priestly colleges on behalf of the state, and by heads of households for their families. Belief mattered less than keeping faith with the gods (pax deorum) through ritual done properly. The major priesthoods, the pontifices headed by the pontifex maximus, the augurs, the Vestal Virgins, and the flamines of individual gods, were held by members of the governing elite.

## Native gods and Greek stories

The earliest Roman gods, Jupiter, Mars, and Quirinus, Janus, Vesta, and many small powers of house and field, had few myths of their own. From an early date Rome absorbed Etruscan and Greek influence: the Capitoline triad of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva had an Etruscan-style temple dedicated, by tradition, in 509 BCE, and Greek gods such as Apollo were adopted outright. Roman writers then identified their gods with the Greek Olympians (Jupiter with Zeus, Juno with Hera, Minerva with Athena), so that much of what is called Roman mythology is Greek mythology told in Latin, above all in Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.

## Rome's own myths

The myths the Romans developed most fully were stories about Rome itself: Aeneas's flight from Troy and his arrival in Latium, told in Virgil's *Aeneid*; Romulus and Remus and the founding of the city, and the early kings, told by Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus; and the origins of festivals and cults, explained in Ovid's *Fasti* and Varro's lost *Antiquities*, known through quotations. These are political myths, tying the gods to the city's history and destiny.

## Change and end

Under the empire the cult of the deified emperors joined the state religion, and cults from the eastern provinces, such as those of Isis, Cybele, and Mithras, spread widely. After Constantine's conversion Christianity was favoured, and laws under Theodosius I in the 390s banned public sacrifice; the fire of Vesta was put out and the Vestals disbanded. The date 476 used here marks the end of the western empire, not a single moment when the old religion ceased.

name: Hindu Pantheon
culture: Hindu/Vedic
description: Hindu mythology encompasses thousands of years of religious and philosophical tradition from the Indian subcontinent. Centered on the Trimurti (Brahma the Creator, Vishnu the Preserver, and Shiva the Destroyer) and featuring countless gods, goddesses, and avatars.
detailedHistory:
## Many texts, many traditions

Hinduism is not a single religion with one founder or scripture but a family of traditions developing over more than three thousand years and practised today by over a billion people. This site's entries follow the principal textual sources while recognising that devotional and regional traditions often tell the stories differently.

## The Vedas

The oldest layer is the *Rigveda*, hymns in Vedic Sanskrit composed in the northwest of the subcontinent in roughly the later second millennium BCE and transmitted orally with extraordinary precision long before being written down. Its prominent gods are Indra, slayer of the serpent Vritra, Agni the fire, Soma, Varuna, and the dawn goddess Ushas; Vishnu and Rudra, later Shiva, are comparatively minor. Later Vedic texts, the Brahmanas and the Upanishads, turned to the meaning of sacrifice and to the identity of the self (atman) with ultimate reality (brahman).

## Epics and Puranas

The two Sanskrit epics, the *Mahabharata*, which contains the *Bhagavad Gita*, and the *Ramayana*, took shape over centuries around the turn of the common era and remain the most widely known stories in South and Southeast Asia. The Puranas, compiled from roughly the 3rd century CE into the second millennium, organise the gods around great deities: Vishnu and his avatars, including Rama and Krishna; Shiva with Parvati and their sons Ganesha and Kartikeya; and the Goddess, Devi, in forms such as Durga and Kali. The idea of the Trimurti, Brahma as creator, Vishnu as preserver, and Shiva as destroyer, is a Puranic scheme; in practice most devotees worship Vishnu, Shiva, or the Goddess as supreme.

## Living worship

Hindu worship centres on temples, household shrines, pilgrimage, and festivals such as Diwali, Holi, and Navaratri. Tamil devotional poetry, regional epics, and local goddess traditions are as much part of Hindu mythology as the Sanskrit texts. The start date of 1500 BCE given here is a conventional marker for the Vedic period; the tradition has no end date.

name: Japanese Pantheon
culture: Shinto/Japanese
description: Shinto (Way of the Kami) is the indigenous spirituality of Japan, featuring countless kami (divine spirits or gods) associated with natural phenomena, ancestors, and sacred places.
detailedHistory:
## Kami

Kami are the sacred powers of Japanese religion: the great deities of the classical myths, but also mountains, waterfalls, ancient trees, ancestors, and remarkable people. Shinto, 'the way of the kami', names the practices that honour them at shrines across Japan. The name took on its modern sense relatively late, and for most of Japanese history kami worship was closely combined with Buddhism, the two separated by government order only in 1868.

## The written myths

The classical myths are known from two court histories compiled in the early 8th century: the *Kojiki* ('Record of Ancient Matters', 712), written down by Ō no Yasumaro, and the *Nihon Shoki* ('Chronicles of Japan', 720), which records many variant versions side by side. Both begin with the creation of the islands by Izanagi and Izanami, tell of Amaterasu, the sun goddess, and her unruly brother Susanoo, the Izumo cycle of Ōkuninushi, and the descent of Amaterasu's grandson Ninigi to rule the land. They then run on into the reigns of legendary and historical emperors. Both were compiled to support the authority of the imperial house, which claims descent from Amaterasu, and they should be read with that purpose in mind. The provincial *Fudoki* gazetteers of the same period preserve local myths the court histories leave out.

## Shrines and practice

The Ise Grand Shrine, dedicated to Amaterasu and rebuilt every twenty years, and Izumo Taisha, dedicated to Ōkuninushi, are the most important shrines associated with the myths. Practice centres on purification, offerings, seasonal festivals (matsuri), and prayer at shrines. The conventional date of 660 BCE for the first emperor, Jimmu, comes from the *Nihon Shoki* and is legendary, not historical.

name: Celtic Pantheon
culture: Celtic
description: The deities of the Celtic peoples, associated with nature, magic, war, and sovereignty. Known for the Tuatha Dé Danann in Irish mythology.
detailedHistory:
## A modern label

'Celtic' is a linguistic term: it groups peoples who spoke Celtic languages, from Gaul and Britain to Ireland, Iberia, and Galatia in Anatolia. There was no single Celtic religion or pantheon. This site's entries draw on two very different bodies of evidence, and it is important to keep them apart.

## Ancient Gaul and Britain

The first is the evidence from the ancient continental Celts and Roman Britain: inscriptions naming hundreds of gods, many of them local, often paired with Roman gods (Sulis Minerva at Bath, Lenus Mars); images such as the antlered god on the Gundestrup cauldron and the Pillar of the Boatmen from Paris, which names Cernunnos; and the reports of Greek and Roman writers. Julius Caesar's *Gallic War* (6.13-18) describes the druids and equates Gaulish gods with Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva, but he was an enemy general writing for Romans. No myths survive from these peoples in their own words.

## Medieval Ireland and Wales

The second is the literature written down by Christian scholars in Ireland from about the 7th century and in Wales later. Irish texts such as the *Lebor Gabála Érenn* (the 'Book of Invasions'), *Cath Maige Tuired*, and the tales of the Ulster Cycle, including the *Táin Bó Cúailnge*, present the Túatha Dé Danann (Dagda, Lug, Brigit, Nuadu, the Morrígan) as a race of ancient rulers who withdrew into the mounds (síde), not openly as gods. The Welsh *Four Branches of the Mabinogi*, preserved in 14th-century manuscripts, include figures such as Rhiannon, Manawydan, and Lleu, whose names echo older deities. How much of this literature preserves pre-Christian belief, and how much is medieval invention, is a long-running scholarly debate.

## Dates

The period of 500 BCE to 400 CE given here covers the Iron Age and Roman evidence; the Irish and Welsh literature was written down centuries after it, and many sites connected with the stories, such as Tara, Newgrange, and Emain Macha, are far older than any text.

name: Aztec Pantheon
culture: Nahua/Aztec
description: A complex pantheon centered on duality, sacrifice, and the sun, demanding blood sacrifice to sustain the cosmos.
detailedHistory:
## The Mexica and their neighbours

'Aztec' usually refers to the Nahuatl-speaking peoples of central Mexico and especially to the Mexica, who founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally in 1325, and, through the Triple Alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, dominated much of Mesoamerica until the Spanish conquest in 1521. Their religion shared a great deal with other Mesoamerican peoples: the 260-day ritual calendar, the ballgame, a layered cosmos of heavens and underworld, and the feathered serpent.

## The sources

Only a handful of pre-conquest manuscripts survive, among them ritual and divinatory books of the Borgia Group from central and southern Mexico. Most of what is known was recorded after 1521. The most important source is the *General History of the Things of New Spain*, the *Florentine Codex*, compiled in Nahuatl and Spanish between the 1540s and about 1577 by the Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún with Nahua scholars and elders. Other key texts include the *Leyenda de los Soles* (1558), the *Historia de los mexicanos por sus pinturas*, the *Histoyre du Mechique*, and illustrated colonial codices such as the *Codex Borbonicus* and *Codex Mendoza*. All were produced under Spanish rule, often by missionaries seeking to understand and suppress the old religion, and their framing needs care.

## Gods and the Fifth Sun

The cosmology tells of four earlier worlds, or suns, each destroyed, before the present Fifth Sun was created at Teotihuacan when the gods Nanahuatzin and Tecuciztecatl threw themselves into a fire. The gods then gave their own blood to set the sun moving, and humans were thought to owe a debt repaid through offerings, including blood and, in state ritual, human sacrifice. Huitzilopochtli, the Mexica patron, and Tlaloc, god of rain, shared the Templo Mayor; Quetzalcoatl, Tezcatlipoca, and many others were worshipped through a year of monthly festivals.

## After 1521

The temples were destroyed, but Nahuatl, the calendar's memory, and many practices continued in altered forms, and Nahua communities today are the descendants of the people who kept these traditions.

name: Chinese Pantheon
culture: Chinese
description: A vast bureaucracy of gods, spirits, and immortals reflecting the imperial government on earth, blending Taoism, Buddhism, and folk religion.
detailedHistory:
## The Celestial Bureaucracy

Chinese mythology is unique in structuring its divine realm as a mirror of the imperial government on Earth. The Jade Emperor presides over a complex hierarchy of gods, spirits, and immortals, each with specific ranks, duties, and jurisdictions. This 'celestial bureaucracy' includes ministries of thunder, rain, fire, and pestilence, with deities promoted or demoted based on their performance.

### Three Traditions United

Chinese mythology synthesizes three major traditions: **Taoism** (with its emphasis on immortality, nature, and the Tao), **Buddhism** (introducing bodhisattvas like Guanyin and concepts of karma), and **folk religion** (featuring local gods, ancestor worship, and nature spirits). This syncretism allows figures like Sun Wukong to be simultaneously a Taoist immortal, a Buddhist disciple, and a folk hero.

### The Quest for Immortality

A central theme is the pursuit of immortality through cultivation (xiu lian). Through meditation, moral conduct, and alchemical practices, mortals can become immortals (xian) and join the celestial hierarchy. This reflects the Taoist belief that the human body can be transformed through spiritual practice.

### Heaven, Earth, and the Underworld

The cosmos is divided into three realms: Heaven (Tian), ruled by the Jade Emperor; Earth (Di), inhabited by humans and nature spirits; and the Underworld (Diyu), governed by Yan Wang (King Yama) where souls are judged and may be punished or reincarnated. The interconnection of these realms drives many myths.

name: Mesopotamian Pantheon
culture: Sumerian, Akkadian, Babylonian
description: The gods of ancient Sumer, Akkad, and Babylon - humanity's oldest recorded mythology. These deities shaped the earliest written literature and influenced all subsequent Near Eastern religions.
detailedHistory:
## The Cradle of Civilization

Mesopotamian mythology represents humanity's oldest recorded religious tradition, emerging from the fertile crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. The Sumerians, who built the first cities around 3500 BCE, developed a complex pantheon that was later adopted and adapted by the Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians.

### The Great Gods

The highest triad consisted of Anu (sky), Enlil (wind/storms), and Enki (water/wisdom). Below them ruled a celestial council of great gods who determined the fates of humans and the cosmos. Unlike later monotheistic traditions, these gods were not morally perfect but displayed human emotions and conflicts.

### The Temple Economy

Mesopotamian cities were theocracies centered on the ziggurat temple, considered the literal dwelling place of the city's patron deity. The entire economy was organized around temple offerings, and kings ruled as stewards of the gods. The earliest written texts (cuneiform) were temple records, hymns, and myths.

name: African Traditions
culture: Several distinct African peoples (Zulu and Xhosa, Swahili, Mandinka, Ewe, Mongo) and the Mami Wata tradition
description: A regional collection, not a pantheon: beings from African traditions that do not yet have their own entry on this site. Yoruba orisha and Akan figures such as Nyame and Anansi now have their own pages.
detailedHistory:
## A collection, not a pantheon

This page used to gather Yoruba orisha, Akan figures, and beings from several other African peoples under one heading. That grouping implied a shared religion that never existed, so the two best-documented traditions now have their own entries, and this page keeps only what remains: creatures and spirits from peoples whose traditions this site has not yet covered in depth. Nothing here implies a common origin, date, or cosmology.

### Yoruba traditions

The orisha of the Yoruba of southwestern Nigeria and neighbouring Benin, with the creation at Ile-Ife, Ifa divination, and the diaspora religions that grew from them, are now on the [Yoruba Tradition](/pantheons/yoruba) page.

### Akan storytelling

Nyame, Asase Yaa, the river abosom, and Kwaku Ananse the spider, known largely through R. S. Rattray's recordings of Asante tellers in the 1920s, are now on the [Akan Tradition](/pantheons/akan) page.

### What stays here

The beings still listed on this page come from separate peoples and should be read that way: the tikoloshe from Zulu and Xhosa belief in South Africa, the popobawa from late-20th-century reports on Zanzibar and Pemba, the ninki-nanka from Mandinka and neighbouring traditions of the Gambia and Senegal, the adze from Ewe belief in Ghana and Togo, and the eloko from the Mongo of the Congo basin. Mami Wata is the exception: a water spirit venerated across West and Central Africa and the diaspora, whose modern image owes much to 19th- and 20th-century trade and print culture. Each entry names the people it belongs to, and none should be read as Yoruba or Akan.

name: Polynesian Pantheon
culture: Polynesian (Hawaiian, Maori, Samoan, Tahitian)
description: The gods and spirits of Polynesian mythology span the vast Pacific Ocean, from Hawaii to New Zealand to Easter Island. Featuring powerful creator gods, the trickster demigod Maui, and deep connections to the sea, navigation, and volcanic forces.
detailedHistory:
## Voyagers of the Pacific

Polynesian mythology developed among the greatest ocean navigators in human history. Beginning around 1500 BCE, Polynesian peoples spread across the Pacific, carrying their gods, stories, and rituals to islands separated by thousands of miles of open ocean.

### The Polynesian Triangle

The Polynesian Triangle stretches from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand (Aotearoa) in the southwest and Easter Island (Rapa Nui) in the southeast. Despite this vast expanse, the mythologies share common roots: the primordial parents Rangi (Sky Father) and Papa (Earth Mother), the great gods Tangaroa, Tane, Tu, and Rongo, and the beloved trickster demigod Maui.

### Regional Variations

While sharing common ancestors, each island group developed distinct traditions. Hawaiian mythology features the volcano goddess Pele and her rivalry with the snow goddess Poliahu. Maori tradition preserves elaborate genealogies (whakapapa) connecting humans to the gods. Samoan and Tongan traditions emphasize Tagaloa as the supreme creator.

### Oral Tradition

Polynesian mythology was preserved through oral tradition, chants (mele in Hawaiian, waiata in Maori), and ritual performances. Navigational knowledge, genealogies, and sacred stories were memorized by specialists and passed down through generations, only being written down after European contact.

name: Mesoamerican Pantheon
culture: Aztec, Maya, and related Mesoamerican traditions
description: Mesoamerican mythology encompasses Aztec, Maya, Olmec, and other pre-Columbian traditions. Featuring feathered serpent deities, cosmic cycles of creation and destruction, underworld journeys, and the belief that sacrifice sustains the universe.
detailedHistory:
## Two Thousand Years of Civilization

Mesoamerican mythology represents one of humanity's most complex and interconnected religious traditions, developing independently in the Americas over millennia. From the Olmec 'mother culture' (1500-400 BCE) through the Maya Classic period (250-900 CE) to the Aztec Empire (1300-1521 CE), these civilizations shared fundamental concepts while developing unique expressions.

### The Feathered Serpent

The figure of the feathered serpent appears throughout Mesoamerican history: as Quetzalcoatl among the Aztecs and Kukulkan among the Maya. This deity represents the union of earth (serpent) and sky (quetzal bird), embodying wind, wisdom, and the morning star. Worship of feathered serpent deities dates back to at least the Olmec era.

### Cycles of Creation and Destruction

Both Aztec and Maya traditions describe multiple world ages or 'suns' that were created and destroyed. The current world exists in a precarious balance, sustained by proper ritual observance. Time itself was cyclical, with elaborate calendars tracking sacred and agricultural cycles.

### The Underworld Journey

The Aztec Mictlan and Maya Xibalba represent perilous underworld realms that souls must traverse after death. The Maya Popol Vuh recounts the Hero Twins' journey to Xibalba, while Aztec mythology describes Quetzalcoatl's descent to Mictlan to retrieve ancestral bones.

### Sacrifice and Cosmic Debt

Mesoamerican religions understood humanity as owing a fundamental debt to the gods who sacrificed themselves to create the current world. This debt could only be repaid through offerings, including blood sacrifice, which was seen as nourishing the cosmos itself.

name: Slavic Pantheon
culture: Slavic (East, West, and Baltic-coast Slavic peoples)
description: The gods of the pre-Christian Slavic peoples, known almost entirely through hostile outside witnesses, a handful of chronicle entries, and the outlines that survived Christianization inside later folklore.
detailedHistory:
## A religion without its own scripture

No native Slavic pagan text survives. Everything known comes from outsiders (a Byzantine soldier-historian, German and Danish churchmen), from a handful of lines in Christian chronicles written after the fact, and from linguistic and archaeological reconstruction. The earliest witness is Procopius, who in his *History of the Wars* (7.14, written in the 550s CE) describes the early Slavs worshipping a single, unnamed god who "master of all" hurls the lightning, and sacrificing cattle and other victims to him, alongside rivers, nymphs, and other spirits that receive lesser offerings. He names no gods.

## East Slavic Rus': the Primary Chronicle

The *Russian Primary Chronicle* (*Povest' vremennykh let*), compiled in Kiev in the early 12th century and preserved in the Laurentian codex (1377) and Hypatian codex (c. 1425), records the treaties of 907, 945, and 971, in which the Rus' swear by their weapons, by Perun, and by Volos (Veles), "the cattle god." Under the year 980 it reports that Prince Vladimir of Kiev set up six idols on a hill outside his palace — Perun, Khors, Dazhbog, Stribog, Simargl, and Mokosh — which he had torn down and thrown into the Dnieper after his own conversion in 988. A separate strand, a gloss inserted into the Hypatian Chronicle's translation of John Malalas under 1114, borrows the frame of Greek mythology to equate Svarog with Hephaestus and to call Dazhbog "son of Svarog" — most historians read this as a learned monk's literary aside, not as direct testimony to living cult.

## West Slavic and Baltic-coast Slavs: temples the Rus' never had

Unlike the Rus', the Polabian and Pomeranian Slavs (the Redarii, the Rani of Rügen, the Pomeranians around Szczecin) built actual temple buildings with carved cult images, and German and Danish churchmen described what they saw before tearing it down: Thietmar of Merseburg (*Chronicon*, completed by 1018) on Svarozhich at the shrine of Riedegost; Adam of Bremen (*Gesta Hammaburgensis Ecclesiae Pontificum*, c. 1075), who gives a different name, Redigast, for what may be the same site; Helmold of Bosau (*Chronica Slavorum*, c. 1168) on Chernobog and on Prove and Svantevit among the Wagrians and Rani; Saxo Grammaticus (*Gesta Danorum*, Book 14, c. 1200–1216) on the four-headed idol and the white divination-horse at Arkona, destroyed by the Danish king Valdemar I in 1168; and the *Lives of Otto of Bamberg* by Ebbo and Herbord (1150s) on Triglav at Szczecin, destroyed during Otto's mission of 1124–1128.

## Reading these sources honestly

Every one of these accounts was written by a Christian outsider recording either conquest or conversion, so hostile framing and outright misunderstanding are built into the record. Vladimir's 980 pantheon was a political act by a reigning prince, not a description of a stable state religion observed from inside. Khors and Simargl are barely understood at all — their names are probably borrowed, and assigning either a confident "domain" goes beyond what the sources support. And the storm-combat between Perun and Veles, often retold on the internet as if it were an attested myth, is a 20th-century linguistic reconstruction by Vyacheslav Ivanov and Vladimir Toporov, built by comparing later folklore, place names, and Baltic and Vedic parallels — not a story any medieval writer set down.

## What this site will not repeat

The *Book of Veles* (*Velesova kniga*), first published in the 1950s and claiming to be an ancient birch-bark chronicle, is a demonstrated 20th-century forgery: its language mixes Slavic forms from different centuries and no physical tablet has ever been produced for inspection. The Prav-Yav-Nav triad and the "god" Chislobog that circulate in popular and Rodnovery (Slavic neopagan) writing come from that forgery or from modern invention, not from any medieval source, and are not treated here as ancient. Figures such as Lada and a personified Kupala are attested only in early-modern and modern folklore, never in a pagan-era source, and are marked as such wherever they appear.

## Folk survival

After Christianization (the Rus' in 988; the Baltic Slavs by the 12th–13th century), older beliefs did not vanish but layered under a Christian surface, a pattern Russian scholarship calls *dvoeverie* ("double-faith"): Perun's thunder role was partly absorbed into the prophet Elijah, Veles's patronage of cattle partly into Saint Blaise, and a rich lower mythology of household, forest, and water spirits (domovoi, leshy, vodyanoy, rusalka) survived into the 19th-century folklore collected by ethnographers such as Alexander Afanasyev — a genuinely rich record, but of 19th-century peasant belief, not of ancient pagan theology.

name: Haudenosaunee Tradition
culture: Haudenosaunee (Six Nations / Iroquois Confederacy: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, Tuscarora)
region: Northeastern Woodlands (present-day New York State and southern Ontario)
description: A living tradition of the sovereign Haudenosaunee nations: Sky Woman's fall to Turtle Island, the twins Sapling and Flint, and the Peacemaker's founding of the Great Law of Peace, told today by the people who tell it.
detailedHistory:
## Two nations, one entry

The Haudenosaunee (People of the Longhouse, also called the Six Nations or, by an exonym, the Iroquois Confederacy) are Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and, since the early 18th century, Tuscarora nations. They are sovereign nations today, with their own governments, and Haudenosaunee people practice, teach, and retell these traditions now, not only in a documented past. This entry follows only what the Confederacy and its constituent nations share publicly themselves, plus scholarship recorded with, or in direct collaboration with, Haudenosaunee tellers, and it leaves out anything described as belonging to a specific medicine society or ceremony.

## Sky Woman, the Twins, and Turtle Island

In Haudenosaunee tradition, in the Sky World above, a woman falls through a hole torn open when a great tree is uprooted. Waterfowl slow her fall and set her on the back of a Great Turtle, who offers to bear the earth; other animals dive into the primordial waters beneath the Turtle to bring up a pawful of mud, which grows across the Turtle's back into the world, later called Turtle Island. Sky Woman's daughter is born on this new earth, and the daughter in turn gives birth to twin grandsons: the good-minded Sapling, also called Skyholder or, among the Mohawk, Teharonhiawagon ("He Holds Up the Sky"), and the hard-minded Flint (Tawiskaron), born in a way that costs their mother's life. Sapling and Flint go on to shape the features of the world, one making it fertile and easy to live in, the other making it difficult, and different nations and tellers place different weight on how their contest ends. This is cosmological tradition, not a dated history; it is told in the present tense by the people who tell it, not assigned a calendar year.

Sources for this material disagree on details large and small: which animal succeeds at diving for the mud (muskrat, in many Seneca and Onondaga tellings), what becomes of the twins' mother, and how firmly Flint is defeated versus simply withdrawn. Arthur C. Parker's *Seneca Myths and Folk Tales* (1923) and J.N.B. Hewitt's *Iroquoian Cosmology* (Bureau of American Ethnology Annual Reports 21 and 43) record these variations from Onondaga, Seneca, and Mohawk tellers by name; Hewitt was himself Tuscarora. This entry follows their lead in presenting variants side by side rather than flattening them into one version.

## The Peacemaker and the Great Law of Peace

A separate, later strand of tradition, one the Confederacy calls history as much as sacred narrative, tells how the Great Law of Peace (Gayanashagowa) brought the warring nations together under a shared government. In the accounts the Onondaga Nation and the Haudenosaunee Confederacy publish on their own websites, the Peacemaker, sent to end the fighting, is joined by Hiawatha (Aiionwatha), an Onondaga man who had lost his family to violence; together they persuade the powerful and feared Onondaga leader Tadodaho, described in both accounts as having snakes in his hair and a twisted body, to accept peace and become the confederacy's Firekeeper. At Onondaga Lake the nations plant the Great Tree of Peace, its roots reaching to the four directions and an eagle set at its top to watch for danger, and the Peacemaker teaches the law of "One Dish, One Spoon" and government by consensus among fifty chiefs.

Historians and the nations themselves date this founding differently: some scholars, working from an oral reference to a solar eclipse, argue for a date around 1142 CE, while archaeological approaches favor a later date, often the 15th century; the Haudenosaunee Confederacy's own materials describe it simply as "over a thousand years ago." This site does not pick a single date and presents it as it is presented by the nations: a founding whose exact year is debated, not a settled fact.

## What this entry leaves out

Material describing ceremonies of the medicine societies, the False Face Society, and other content the Haudenosaunee themselves mark as restricted or clan-specific is not included here, in line with the guidance of the sources this entry draws on. Nothing here claims to be the single correct version of any story; where tellers differ, that difference is the point.

name: Tlingit and Haida Tradition
culture: Tlingit and Haida (Northwest Coast peoples of present-day Southeast Alaska and Haida Gwaii, British Columbia)
description: A living Northwest Coast tradition of the Tlingit and Haida nations, centered on Raven: stealing daylight from a wealthy old man's boxes, and freeing the first people from a clamshell on the beach at Haida Gwaii.
detailedHistory:
## Two nations, one entry, carefully framed

Tlingit and Haida are distinct nations of the Northwest Coast, the Tlingit centered in what is now Southeast Alaska and the Haida on Haida Gwaii (formerly the Queen Charlotte Islands) in British Columbia and in southern Alaska. Both are living, sovereign peoples, and Raven's stories are told by their own tellers today, not only recorded in old books. Archaeological evidence, karst-cave finds on Haida Gwaii and remains from On Your Knees Cave in Southeast Alaska, documents human presence on this coast for at least 10,000 to 13,000 years; that figure describes how long people have lived here, not the age of any single story, since these are living oral traditions passed down and retold, not artifacts with a fixed date of composition.

## Clan property and what this site includes

Among the Tlingit especially, many stories, crests, and songs are at.óow: property owned by a specific clan, whose telling in full ceremonial context requires that clan's standing and permission. What follows here are Raven-cycle stories in the form they have been published for a general public audience, by the tellers' own nations or with their direct involvement (Sealaska Heritage Institute, the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian nations' own cultural institution, publishes Raven stories for exactly this kind of public telling) or recorded by name from specific tellers by early ethnographers. Nothing describing a restricted ceremony or a clan's exclusive at.óow is included.

## Raven

Raven, Yéil in Tlingit and, in Haida, Xuuya or Yáahl depending on dialect (Skidegate and Masset), is the central figure of this cycle: not a simple trickster but, as the poet and translator Robert Bringhurst put it of the Haida telling, one who "never actually creates anything; he made the world by stealing, exchanging, redistributing, and generally moving things around." Raven steals daylight from an old man's nested boxes at the head of the Nass River in the best-known Tlingit telling, and in a Haida telling recorded by John R. Swanton and reinterpreted in Bill Reid's sculpture *The Raven and the First Men* (1978 to 1980, Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia), he coaxes the first people out of a clamshell on the beach at Rose Spit on Haida Gwaii.

## Sources used here, and how they differ

John R. Swanton's *Tlingit Myths and Texts* (1909) and *Haida Texts and Myths* (1905) are outsider recordings, made by a non-Native ethnographer, but they record specific named Tlingit and Haida tellers and remain the fullest early written source for many of these stories. Nora Marks Dauenhauer and Richard Dauenhauer's *Haa Shuká, Our Ancestors: Tlingit Oral Narratives* (1987), edited with extensive Tlingit-language and cultural annotation, and Robert Bringhurst's translations of the Haida poets Skaay and Ghandl in *A Story as Sharp as a Knife* (1999) represent later, more collaborative scholarship, though Bringhurst's own standing to translate Haida oral literature has itself been debated within Haida and academic communities, and this site notes that debate rather than treating his translations as beyond question. Tellings differ across nation, dialect, and individual teller on details as basic as Raven's kin and exact route to the light; this entry does not force them into a single version.

name: Yoruba Tradition
culture: Yoruba (southwestern Nigeria, Benin, and Togo) and the Orisha religions of the diaspora
description: The orisha of Yoruba religion, a living tradition centred on Ile-Ife: Olodumare above, Obatala and Oduduwa at the making of the land, Orunmila and Ifa divination, and orisha such as Ogun, Shango, Oshun, and Yemoja who crossed the Atlantic into Santería, Candomblé, and related faiths.
detailedHistory:
## A living religion

Yoruba religion is practised today in Nigeria, Benin, and Togo, and, through the forced migration of the Atlantic slave trade, in Cuban Santería (Regla de Ocha), Brazilian Candomblé, Trinidadian Orisha worship, and communities across the Americas. It has no single scripture and no single orthodoxy: each orisha is worshipped through particular lineages, towns, and houses, and practice differs from one to the next. This page presents what published sources and practitioners share publicly, and notes where houses and tellers disagree.

## Olodumare and the orisha

Olodumare (also Olorun, 'owner of the sky') is the supreme being, remote from daily worship and approached through the orisha. The orisha are many (tradition speaks of 401, or of 'countless') and include deities who were present at creation, such as Obatala, and deified ancestors and kings, such as Shango, remembered as a king of Oyo. Eshu carries sacrifice and messages between people and the orisha and must be acknowledged first; Orunmila is the witness of destiny whose wisdom speaks through Ifa.

## Ile-Ife and the making of the land

Creation stories centre on Ile-Ife, regarded as the place where the land was first spread over the primordial waters. Tellings disagree on the central actor: in many, Obatala is sent down a chain from the sky with earth in a snail shell and a five-toed hen to scatter it, but falls asleep drunk on palm wine, and Oduduwa completes the task and becomes the first ruler of Ife. Samuel Johnson's *The History of the Yorubas* (completed 1897, published 1921) records the Oyo tradition; Ife's own traditions give Oduduwa greater weight. The disagreement is itself historical evidence of rival centres, and this site presents both.

## Ifa

Ifa divination, inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (2008), is a vast oral literature of verses (ese) organised into 256 signs (odu). A babalawo casts palm nuts or a divining chain and recites the verses of the resulting sign, many of which contain the myths summarised on this site. Wande Abimbola's editions and translations of Ifa verses (1970s onward) are among the most important published records.

## Dates

The tradition has no founding date. Ile-Ife was a major urban and artistic centre by about the 11th to 15th centuries CE, the period of its celebrated copper-alloy and terracotta heads, but those dates belong to the city and its art, not to the beginning of the religion.

name: Akan Tradition
culture: Akan (Asante, Bono, Fante, Akuapem, and related peoples)
description: The sky god Nyame and the earth Asase Yaa, the river abosom such as Tano, and Kwaku Ananse the spider, who bought the world's stories from Nyame: the religious and storytelling tradition of the Akan peoples of Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.
detailedHistory:
## Sky, earth, and the abosom

Akan religion recognises a supreme sky god, Nyame (also Onyame or Onyankopon), and the earth, Asase Yaa, who is honoured rather than served through shrines and priests. Between people and the sky god stand the abosom, powers associated with rivers, lakes, and other features of the land, such as Tano of the Tano River, and the ancestors (nsamanfo), whose presence is central to Akan religious and political life. Akan religion is a living tradition in Ghana today, alongside Christianity and Islam.

## Rattray and the record

Much of the written record comes from R. S. Rattray, a British colonial anthropologist in the Gold Coast, whose *Ashanti* (1923), *Religion and Art in Ashanti* (1927), and *Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales* (1930) recorded Asante belief and storytelling, the last with the Twi text beside the English. Rattray worked through colonial structures and his interpretations should be read critically, but the tales he printed were told to him by named and unnamed Akan speakers. Akan scholars such as J. B. Danquah, in *The Akan Doctrine of God* (1944), wrote about the same tradition from within it.

## Anansesem

Akan folktales are called anansesem, 'spider stories', whether or not Kwaku Ananse appears in them, because of the tale Rattray printed as the account of how all stories came to belong to the spider: Ananse buys them from Nyame by capturing the python, the leopard, the hornets, and the forest fairy. Tellings traditionally open and close with set formulas disclaiming literal truth. Ananse stories travelled with enslaved Akan people to the Caribbean and the Americas, where he survives as Anansi, Anancy, and Aunt Nancy.

## Dates

The tradition has no recorded founding date; Akan states such as Bono and later Asante emerged between roughly the 13th and 18th centuries, but the religion is older than any one state and this site does not assign it a start year.

name: Hittite Pantheon
culture: Hittite, with Hattian, Hurrian, and Luwian strands (Late Bronze Age Anatolia)
description: The "thousand gods of Hatti": the layered pantheon of the Hittite kingdom, where a native storm-god and sun-goddess stood beside Hattian local deities and Hurrian gods whose myths, the Song of Kumarbi and the Song of Ullikummi, were translated into Hittite at the capital Hattusa.
detailedHistory:
## A pantheon assembled, not inherited

The Hittite kings of the Late Bronze Age (from about 1650 BCE until the collapse of the kingdom around 1180 BCE) ruled from Hattusa, near modern Boğazkale in central Türkiye, and their scribes spoke of "the thousand gods of Hatti" when they listed the divine witnesses to a treaty. The phrase was not an exaggeration so much as an honest description of how the pantheon was built: the Hittites, speakers of an Indo-European language, settled among the Hattians, a non-Indo-European people whose gods (the Storm-god of Nerik, the Sun-goddess of Arinna, Telipinu, Inara) they kept; they absorbed Luwian and Palaic deities from neighbouring Anatolian peoples; and from the fifteenth century BCE onward they took in the gods of the Hurrians of northern Syria and Mesopotamia, including Teššub, Hebat, Šauška, and Kumarbi. Rather than replacing local gods, Hittite religion tended to add them, so that the same storm-god might be worshipped under a Hattian, a Hittite, and a Hurrian name in different rites.

## Where the myths come from, and why that matters

Almost everything on this site about Hittite myth comes from clay tablets excavated at Hattusa since 1906, the archive that allowed Bedřich Hrozný to identify Hittite as an Indo-European language in 1915. Two very different kinds of story survive. The Illuyanka tales and the myth of Telipinu's disappearance are **Anatolian and Hattian** in origin, and they survive because they were written down as part of rituals and festivals: the Illuyanka story was recited at the Purulli festival of Nerik, and the Telipinu story sits inside an invocation meant to coax an angry god home. The Song of Kumarbi, the Song of Ullikummi, and the Song of Hedammu, by contrast, are **Hurrian** literary compositions translated into Hittite; Hurrian-language fragments of the same cycle also survive, and its gods, places, and even its hero Teššub are Hurrian. Modern scholars group these songs as the Kumarbi cycle. This site marks the difference on every story, because treating Hurrian songs as native Hittite myth, a common simplification, hides how the pantheon was actually put together.

## Fragmentary texts

Nearly every one of these compositions is broken. Tablets are damaged, columns are missing, and several endings, including the end of the Song of Ullikummi, are simply lost. Where this site retells a story, it follows the translations of Harry A. Hoffner Jr. (*Hittite Myths*, 2nd ed., 1998) and marks gaps as gaps rather than filling them from later Greek parallels. Text numbers in the *Catalogue des Textes Hittites* (CTH), the standard reference system for Hittite compositions, are given so readers can find each text in any modern edition.

## Why Hittite myth matters beyond Anatolia

The Kumarbi cycle's succession of sky-kings (Alalu, then Anu, then Kumarbi, then the storm-god) and its castration and swallowing episodes are the closest known Near Eastern parallel to Hesiod's *Theogony*, and the storm-god's battle with the serpent Illuyanka belongs to a wide family of storm-god-versus-serpent stories stretching from Ugarit to Scandinavia. This site notes those parallels where they are well established, while treating the Hittite and Hurrian texts on their own terms first.

name: Canaanite Pantheon (Ugarit)
culture: West Semitic (Canaanite), known chiefly from the Ugaritic texts of Ras Shamra
region: The Levant (coastal Syria, Lebanon, and Israel/Palestine)
description: The gods of the Late Bronze Age Levant as the clay tablets of Ugarit preserve them: aged El and Lady Athirat at the head of the divine family, and the storm-god Baal, who defeats the Sea, builds his palace on Mount Zaphon, and is swallowed by Death before he returns.
detailedHistory:
## Ugarit and the problem of the word "Canaanite"

Almost everything known in detail about the myths of the ancient Levant before the first millennium BCE comes from one city: Ugarit, on the Syrian coast at Ras Shamra, north of modern Latakia. In 1928 a farmer's plough broke into a tomb nearby; excavations led by Claude Schaeffer from 1929 uncovered a wealthy port city, destroyed around 1185 BCE, and archives written in a previously unknown alphabetic cuneiform of thirty signs. The mythological poems on this site come from those archives. "Canaanite" is the conventional scholarly label for the shared West Semitic religion of the Levant, and it is used here for that reason; but the people of Ugarit did not call themselves Canaanites (an Ugaritic text lists a "Canaanite" as a foreigner), and the Ugaritic myths should not be assumed to describe every Levantine city. Where later Phoenician or biblical evidence differs, this site says so.

## The texts and their scribe

The three great narrative poems, the Baal Cycle (KTU 1.1-1.6), the Epic of Aqhat (KTU 1.17-1.19), and the Epic of Kirta (KTU 1.14-1.16), survive on tablets copied in the late thirteenth or early twelfth century BCE. Several carry a colophon naming the scribe Ilimilku, who worked under a king Niqmaddu, although the poems themselves are older. All are damaged: whole columns are missing, the order of the Baal tablets is partly reconstructed, and the endings of Aqhat and Kirta are lost. Citations here use the standard KTU numbering (Keilalphabetische Texte aus Ugarit, also published in English as CAT), by tablet and column, so readers can check any retelling against a modern translation such as those of Mark S. Smith, Simon B. Parker, Edward L. Greenstein, and Nicolas Wyatt.

## The divine family

At the head of the pantheon stands El (Ilu), the aged "Father of Years" and "Bull El", creator of creatures, who presides over the assembly of the gods from his dwelling at the source of the two rivers. His consort is Athirat, "Lady Athirat of the Sea", mother of the seventy gods. The drama of the myths, though, belongs to a younger generation: Baal (Baʿlu Haddu), the storm-god of rain and fertility, "Rider of the Clouds", who is called the son of Dagan; his fierce sister-ally Anat; the Sea (Yamm) and Death (Mot), both favourites of El; the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis; and the sun-goddess Shapash, who sees everything as she crosses the sky and the underworld.

## Why these texts matter

The Ugaritic poems are the closest surviving literary context for the Hebrew Bible's poetry. Biblical texts use the same divine names (El, Baal, Asherah), the same image of a storm-god riding the clouds, and even nearly the same words: Isaiah 27:1 describes "Leviathan the twisting serpent" in terms close to the Ugaritic description of Litan. The relationship is one of shared language and imagery across a region, not of one text copying another, and this site describes Ugaritic religion on its own terms rather than as background to the Bible. Readers of Jewish and Christian scripture should also know that biblical polemic against "Baal" and "Asherah" was written centuries later and from a very different standpoint; the Ugaritic texts are the only surviving account of these gods from their own worshippers.

name: Inuit Tradition
culture: Inuit (Inuit Nunangat in Canada, Kalaallit Nunaat/Greenland, and Iñupiat Alaska), with strong regional variation
region: The Arctic, from northern Alaska across Canada to Greenland
description: A living Arctic tradition whose powers go by different names from region to region: the Sea Woman who keeps the sea animals (Sedna, Nuliajuk, Takannaaluk, Sassuma Arnaa), the Moon Man and Sun Woman, and Sila, the breath of the world, told by Inuit from Alaska to Greenland.
detailedHistory:
## One people, many regions, many names

Inuit live across the Arctic: in Inuit Nunangat in Canada (the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut, Nunavik, and Nunatsiavut), in Kalaallit Nunaat (Greenland), and, as Iñupiat, in northern Alaska. They share a language family and a great deal of story, but not a single scripture or standardised mythology. The same figure goes by different names from one region to the next, and the stories told about her differ too. The Sea Woman whom Franz Boas recorded as **Sedna** in Cumberland Sound on Baffin Island in the 1880s is **Nuliajuk** among the Netsilingmiut, **Takannaaluk** or **Uinigumasuittuq** in Iglulik tellings, and **Sassuma Arnaa**, "mother of the deep", in West Greenland. "Sedna" has become the name the wider world knows, even giving its name to a distant dwarf planet, but it is one regional name among many, and this site gives the others alongside it wherever they are known.

## A living tradition

These are not the beliefs of a vanished people. Inuit elders, storytellers, artists, and publishers tell these stories today, in Inuktitut and other Inuit languages as well as in English, Danish, and French. Many Inuit are also Christian, and communities and families hold a wide range of views about the old powers and about the angakkuit (shamans) who once dealt with them. The dates attached to this entry reflect archaeology, not the age of any story: the ancestors of today's Inuit, known to archaeologists as the Thule people, spread east from Alaska across the Arctic from roughly 1000 to 1300 CE, meeting the earlier Arctic people whom Inuit tradition remembers as the Tuniit.

## Sources and their limits

Much of what outsiders know comes from ethnographers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: Franz Boas's *The Central Eskimo* (1888), Hinrich Rink's Greenland collections, and above all the reports of the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921-24) led by Knud Rasmussen, who was himself of Greenlandic Inuit and Danish descent and recorded the words of named Inuit speakers such as Aua in Iglulik and Orpingalik among the Netsilingmiut. These books preserve invaluable testimony, but they also use terms, including "Eskimo", that many Inuit now reject, and they reflect the interests of their compilers. This site recommends reading them alongside Inuit-authored and community-led work: the Nunavut Arctic College series *Interviewing Inuit Elders*, in which Inuit students interviewed elders about their own knowledge; the books of Inhabit Media, an Inuit-owned publisher in Iqaluit; and the films of Isuma and other Inuit filmmakers.

## What this site includes

The stories here are ones that Inuit elders and Inuit-led publishers have made public and that appear in published sources. They are summarised, not presented as authoritative scripts, and details that concern the practice of angakkuuniq (shamanism) are described only in general terms. Where a story differs by region, the differences are the point, not an obstacle to be smoothed away.

name: Aboriginal Australian Traditions
culture: Many distinct Aboriginal nations and language groups; this entry draws on publicly shared stories of the Kulin nations, the Ngemba and Wiradjuri, the Whadjuk Noongar, the Aṉangu, and the Martu, Ngaanyatjarra, and Aṉangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara peoples
description: Not one mythology but the living laws and stories of hundreds of Aboriginal nations, often called the Dreaming in English. This entry is a respectful introduction limited to stories that their custodians have chosen to share publicly, each attributed to its people and Country.
detailedHistory:
## A cultural note before reading

This entry includes only stories that Aboriginal custodians have chosen to share publicly, in forms published by or with the communities concerned: through national park signage written with traditional owners, national heritage listings prepared in consultation with communities, museum exhibitions developed with knowledge holders, and community organisations' own publications. Much Aboriginal knowledge is secret or sacred, restricted by gender, age, or initiation, or belongs to particular families and clans; none of that material is included here, and where a figure is associated with restricted ceremony, this site says so and stops. Summaries on this site are not a substitute for the tellings of the peoples themselves, and readers are encouraged to seek out community-authored sources, such as the publications of Aboriginal land councils and cultural centres, the First Knowledges book series, and works by Aboriginal authors.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that sources linked from this entry may contain names and images of people who have died.

## Not one mythology

Before colonisation there were more than 250 Aboriginal languages and many more dialects, each the language of a people with its own Country, law, and stories. There is no single "Aboriginal mythology", any more than there is a single European one, and presenting Kulin, Noongar, and Aṉangu stories on one page does not mean they belong to one system. Each story on this site is attributed to the people and Country it belongs to. Torres Strait Islander peoples have their own distinct traditions, which this entry does not cover.

## The Dreaming, and the words for it

"The Dreaming" and "Dreamtime" are English words, popularised by the anthropologists Baldwin Spencer and Francis Gillen from an Arrernte term, and by W. E. H. Stanner's essay "The Dreaming" (1953). Aboriginal languages have their own terms, with their own meanings: Jukurrpa in Warlpiri, Tjukurpa for Aṉangu, Altyerre in Arrernte, Nyitting for Noongar people, and many others. These words name something that is not simply a distant past: ancestral beings travelled and shaped the land, established law, and remain present in Country, in the stars, and in the lives of their descendants. Stanner's word for this was "everywhen". This entry therefore does not give a start or end date.

## Not "gods"

The beings on this page are called ancestral beings or creator beings, not gods. Some, like Bunjil and Baiame, were described by nineteenth-century missionaries and ethnographers as a "Supreme Being" or "All-Father", and scholars have long debated how much those descriptions were shaped by Christian expectations. Others, like the Seven Sisters or Kuniya and Liru, are ancestors whose actions left their marks on the land. The site's usual "deity" format is used for technical reasons only, and each figure is labelled as an ancestral being.

## Songlines and Country

Many ancestral journeys are recorded as songlines: sequences of songs, stories, dances, and designs that follow the ancestors' tracks across the land, sometimes for thousands of kilometres and through the Countries of many peoples. A songline is at once a map, a law, and a history. The Seven Sisters songline shared through the National Museum of Australia's exhibition *Songlines: Tracking the Seven Sisters* (2017) is one publicly shared example.

## Colonisation and continuity

Colonisation from 1788 brought dispossession, violence, the removal of children, and the suppression of languages and ceremonies. Aboriginal law and story nonetheless continue, held by elders, taught in communities, and increasingly shared on Aboriginal terms, as in the co-management of Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park and the National Heritage listing of Baiame's Ngunnhu at Brewarrina. The recognition of Aboriginal cultural authority over these stories is part of that continuing history.

name: Diné (Navajo) Tradition
culture: Diné (Navajo), within Diné Bikéyah, the land between the four sacred mountains
region: Diné Bikéyah (the Navajo Nation and surrounding lands of the Four Corners region, southwestern United States)
description: The living tradition of the Diné, the People, whose Holy People (Diyin Dineʼé) include Changing Woman, the Hero Twins Monster Slayer and Born for Water, First Man and First Woman, Spider Woman, and Coyote; told here only at summary level, with seasonal and ceremonial restrictions respected.
detailedHistory:
## A note on telling these stories

The stories on this page are sacred narratives of a living people. Many Diné families teach that Coyote stories, and much of the account of the emergence and the Holy People, should be told only in winter, after the first frost and before the thunder of spring; telling them out of season can be harmful. Diné scholars, including the historian Jennifer Nez Denetdale, have also cautioned that outsiders' retellings have often distorted Diné history and religion, stripped stories of their ceremonial context, or treated them as quaint folklore. This site therefore keeps retellings short and at the level of published summaries, attributes them to their sources, does not describe ceremonies, and does not reproduce sandpaintings or ceremonial images; the plates on these pages are deliberately plain placeholders. Readers are encouraged to learn from Diné-authored works and Diné institutions such as Diné College and the Navajo Nation Museum.

## The Diné and Diné Bikéyah

The Diné (the People), known in English as the Navajo, are one of the largest Native nations in the United States; the Navajo Nation's land spans parts of Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. Diné Bikéyah, Diné land, is bounded by four sacred mountains: Sisnaajiní (Blanca Peak) in the east, Tsoodził (Mount Taylor) in the south, Dookʼoʼoosłííd (the San Francisco Peaks) in the west, and Dibé Ntsaa (Hesperus Mountain) in the north. Within them lie other sacred places, including Dziłnaʼoodiłii (Huerfano Mountain) and Chʼóolʼį́ʼí (Gobernador Knob), where Changing Woman was found. Archaeologists and linguists relate the Diné to other Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the north; Diné tradition tells of an emergence into this world from worlds below. This site does not set one account against the other, and gives no start date.

## The Holy People

The Diyin Dineʼé, Holy People, are powerful beings who shaped the world and gave the Diné their way of life; the Diné are the Earth Surface People (Nihookáá Dineʼé). "Holy" here means powerful and to be approached carefully, not necessarily good: Coyote is among the Holy People, and so are beings who caused harm. Central to Diné thought is hózhó, often translated as beauty, harmony, or balance, which ceremonies seek to restore.

## Sources and their limits

The best-known published sources were produced by outsiders. Washington Matthews, a U.S. Army surgeon who worked with Diné ceremonial practitioners in the 1880s, published *Navaho Legends* in 1897, a translation of the origin story and related narratives in the orthography of his day. Paul G. Zolbrod's *Diné bahaneʼ: The Navajo Creation Story* (1984) reworked Matthews's material and other sources into a continuous English narrative, and has itself been criticised by Diné readers for presenting a composite as if it were one authoritative telling. Diné-authored works include *Navajo History* (1971), produced by the Navajo Curriculum Center at Rough Rock Demonstration School, and essays gathered in *Diné Perspectives: Revitalizing and Reclaiming Navajo Thought* (2014, edited by Lloyd L. Lee). Accounts vary by family, clan, and ceremonial tradition, and differences between versions are not errors.

name: Inca and Andean Tradition
culture: Inca (Tawantinsuyu) and the wider Quechua- and Aymara-speaking Andean world
description: The religion of the Inca state and the older Andean shrines it absorbed: Viracocha the maker rising from Lake Titicaca, Inti the Sun as ancestor of the Inca kings, and the mountain and coastal huacas of the Huarochirí Manuscript, all known through writers of the colonial era.
detailedHistory:
## Known only through the colonial filter

The Incas kept records on knotted cords (khipu) read by trained specialists, but they left no written narratives of their gods. Every story on this site was written down after the Spanish invasion of 1532, by people with their own purposes. Juan de Betanzos (1551) wrote in Cusco with the help of his wife's royal Inca kin. Cristóbal de Molina (c. 1575) questioned elders who had served in the state cult. Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa (1572) interviewed Inca lineage heads for a viceroy who wanted the Incas shown as tyrants. The Inca Garcilaso de la Vega (1609), son of a Spanish captain and an Inca noblewoman, wrote from Spain decades later and presented Inca religion as a noble monotheism that anticipated Christianity. Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala (c. 1615), an Andean noble, drew and wrote a long protest to the Spanish king. And much of what survives about local gods comes from the campaigns to destroy them: the Quechua Huarochirí Manuscript (c. 1598-1608) was compiled in the circle of the extirpator Francisco de Ávila. Each of these sources is used here for what it can show, with its point of view stated.

## Two layers: the state cult and the huacas

At the top of the Inca state cult stood the Creator (called Viracocha, Con Tici Viracocha, or Pachayachachic), the Sun (Inti), the Thunder (Illapa), and the Moon (Mama Killa), whose images and chambers were housed in the Coricancha, the gold-sheathed temple at the center of Cusco. Beneath and alongside them were countless huacas: mountains, springs, stones, ancestral mummies, and regional gods with their own priests, oracles, and stories, such as Pachacamac on the coast and Pariacaca in the highlands of Huarochirí. The Inca state generally absorbed these rather than abolishing them, adding a Temple of the Sun beside Pachacamac's ancient shrine, for example, and keeping the images of conquered peoples' huacas in Cusco. Around Cusco itself, the Jesuit Bernabé Cobo later listed more than three hundred shrines arranged along imaginary lines (ceques) radiating from the Coricancha.

## Origins, ancestors, and the Sun

The Inca kings claimed descent from the Sun through the founding ancestor Manco Cápac. Chroniclers preserve two main versions of that origin: in one, told by Garcilaso, the Sun sends his son and daughter to Lake Titicaca to civilize humanity; in the other, told by Betanzos and Sarmiento, four brothers and four sisters emerge from a cave at Pacaritambo and travel to the valley of Cusco. Andean peoples more generally traced each lineage to a pacarina, a place of emergence such as a lake, spring, or cave.

## After 1572, and today

The Inca state ended with the fall of Vilcabamba and the execution of Túpac Amaru in 1572, when the Sun image called the Punchao was also captured. Andean religion did not end with it. Quechua and Aymara communities continue to make offerings to Pachamama and to the mountain lords (apus), often alongside Catholic practice, and the Inti Raymi solstice pageant has been re-staged at Sacsayhuamán in Cusco since 1944 as a civic festival reconstructed largely from Garcilaso's description.

name: Persian (Iranian) Tradition
culture: Ancient Iranian: Avestan and Zoroastrian religion, the Achaemenid and Sasanian empires, and the Persian epic tradition
description: The divine beings and heroes of ancient Iran in two distinct layers: the Zoroastrian scripture of the Avesta, with Ahura Mazda, Angra Mainyu, Mithra, and Anahita, and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, which a thousand years later retold Iran's primeval kings and heroes as epic.
detailedHistory:
## Two traditions, kept apart

This entry draws on two bodies of material that should not be blurred together. The first is the **Avesta**, the scripture of Zoroastrianism, composed in Avestan, an Old Iranian language close to the Sanskrit of the Rigveda. Its oldest part, the **Gathas**, are seventeen hymns attributed to the prophet Zarathushtra; their date is disputed, with most scholars placing them somewhere between about 1500 and 1000 BCE on linguistic grounds and others later. The younger parts include the **Yashts**, hymns to individual divine beings such as Mithra, Anahita, and the star Tishtrya, and the **Vendidad**, a book of purity law that preserves myths of creation and of the first king, Yima. The Avesta was transmitted orally for many centuries, written down in a script devised in the Sasanian period, and survives only in medieval manuscripts. Middle Persian books of the ninth and tenth centuries CE, above all the **Bundahishn**, systematize its cosmology.

The second is the **Shahnameh** ('Book of Kings'), the Persian epic completed by Ferdowsi in 1010 CE, in Islamic-era Iran, from older chronicles of the Iranian kings. It contains no gods: Ferdowsi was a Muslim, and the Avestan figures reappear transformed into kings and villains, so that Yima becomes King Jamshid and the three-headed dragon Azhi Dahaka becomes the serpent-shouldered tyrant Zahhak. Its great heroes, Rostam above all, have no clear Avestan counterparts. Each record on this site says which layer it comes from.

## One God, and beings worthy of worship

Zoroastrianism is a living religion, and 'pantheon' fits it only loosely. Zoroastrians today regard **Ahura Mazda**, the Wise Lord, as the one uncreated God. The **Amesha Spentas** ('Beneficent Immortals') such as Spenta Armaiti are his emanations or aspects, and the **yazatas** ('beings worthy of worship') such as Mithra, Anahita, and Tishtrya are divine beings created by him and honored in their own hymns. Opposed to this good creation is **Angra Mainyu** (Ahriman), the Hostile Spirit, who is not a god to be worshipped but the source of death, lies, and every corruption. At the heart of the Gathas is the choice between truth (*asha*) and the lie (*druj*) that each person must make.

## Kings and inscriptions

The Achaemenid kings (550-330 BCE) credited their rule to 'the favor of Ahuramazda' in inscriptions at Behistun, Persepolis, and Naqsh-e Rostam; Artaxerxes II (r. 404-358 BCE) is the first king whose inscriptions also name Anahita and Mithra. Herodotus reports that the Persians worshipped without temples or statues, on the tops of mountains. Under the Sasanians (224-651 CE) Zoroastrianism became a state church with great fire temples, and a speculative current, Zurvanism, made Infinite Time the father of both spirits. After the Arab conquest the religion became a minority in Iran; many Zoroastrians migrated to India, where they are known as Parsis. Zoroastrian communities survive today in Iran, India, and a worldwide diaspora, and festivals rooted in the old calendar, above all **Nowruz**, the new year at the spring equinox, are celebrated across the Iranian world.

## Cautions

The winged figure in a disc on Achaemenid reliefs, now called the Faravahar, is popularly identified with Ahura Mazda, but scholars disagree whether it represents the god, the royal glory, or the king's guardian spirit. The Mithras of the Roman mystery cult shares a name with the Iranian Mithra, but how much, if anything, of Iranian belief lay behind the Roman mysteries remains debated.

name: Finnish Tradition (Kalevala)
culture: Finnish and Karelian (Baltic Finnic) peoples
description: The gods and heroes of Finnish and Karelian runo-song, known from Mikael Agricola's list of 1551, from thousands of folk poems collected in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and above all from Elias Lönnrot's national epic, the Kalevala.
detailedHistory:
## A tradition recorded late

The Baltic Finnic peoples, ancestors of the Finns, Karelians, and Estonians, had no writing before Christianization, which reached Finland gradually between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries through Swedish and Novgorodian influence. The earliest written list of Finnish gods comes from the Lutheran reformer Mikael Agricola, who prefaced his Finnish Psalter of 1551 with a rhymed catalog of the 'idols' of the Tavastians and Karelians: Tapio who gave game from the forest, Ahti who brought fish from the water, Väinämöinen who made songs, Ilmarinen who made calm and storm, Ukko whose bowl was drunk at the spring sowing, and many more. Christfrid Ganander's *Mythologia Fennica* (1789) added a dictionary of beliefs and names.

## Runo-song

The richest evidence is oral poetry in the Kalevala metre, a trochaic line with heavy alliteration and parallelism, sung in Finland, Karelia, and Ingria. It includes epic songs about Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen, and Lemminkäinen, charms (*loitsut*) that invoke the origin of iron, fire, or disease to gain power over it, lyric songs, and wedding songs. The tradition survived longest among the Orthodox Karelians of Viena (White Sea) Karelia, now in Russia. Collected from the late eighteenth century on, these songs fill the 34 volumes of *Suomen Kansan Vanhat Runot*.

## Lönnrot's Kalevala

The physician Elias Lönnrot made eleven collecting journeys between 1828 and 1844, meeting singers such as Arhippa Perttunen of Latvajärvi in Viena Karelia. From his own and others' collections he compiled the *Kalevala* (1835; expanded edition of 50 runes, 1849), joining separate songs into a continuous epic, harmonizing names, supplying linking passages, and sometimes moving episodes between characters. The creation from the eggs, for example, is laid on the knee of Väinämöinen himself in most folk variants; Lönnrot gave the role to the air-maiden he named Ilmatar. The Kalevala is therefore both a work of genuine folk poetry and a nineteenth-century literary creation, and it shaped Finnish national identity during the period of Russian rule before independence in 1917.

## What this entry does

Each record here says whether it rests on Agricola, on folk poetry, or on the Kalevala as Lönnrot arranged it. Quotations from the Kalevala are from John Martin Crawford's public-domain English translation of 1888, which follows the 50-rune edition.

name: Korean Tradition
culture: Korean: the foundation myths of the Three Kingdoms and the shamanic (muism) narrative tradition
description: The founders and gods of Korean tradition: Dangun, born of the Lord of Heaven's son and a bear who became a woman; the egg-born kings Jumong and Bak Hyeokgeose; and the goddesses and creators of shamanic song, such as Princess Bari, guide of the dead, and Mireuk, who separated heaven from earth.
detailedHistory:
## Two bodies of myth

Korean myth reaches us through two very different channels. The first is the **foundation myths** of the ancient kingdoms, written in Literary Chinese by later historians and monks. The earliest datable text is the stele erected in 414 CE for King Gwanggaeto of Goguryeo, whose opening lines tell of the founder Chumo (Jumong), son of the Heavenly Emperor and the River Earl's daughter, breaking out of an egg. Kim Busik's official *Samguk Sagi* (1145) gives full accounts of the founders of Silla, Goguryeo, and Baekje, and the monk Iryeon's *Samguk Yusa* (c. 1281-1289) preserves the earliest surviving telling of the Dangun myth, citing an older record now lost. These texts were written centuries after the events they describe, by scholars with Confucian or Buddhist commitments, and their dates for legendary kings are traditional rather than historical.

The second channel is **muga**, the narrative songs of Korean shamans (*mudang*), performed in rituals (*gut*) and transmitted orally until folklorists began recording them in the twentieth century. They include creation songs in which the deities Mireuk and Seokga contend for the world, and the long narrative of Princess Bari, the abandoned daughter who becomes the guide of the dead. Each song exists in many regional versions; on Jeju Island a distinct body of shamanic myths (*bonpuri*) survives.

## Heaven, founders, and descent

A recurring pattern links the foundation myths: a heavenly figure descends to a mountain or river, unites with an earthly woman associated with animals, water, or the land, and their child founds a kingdom. Hwanung descends to Mount Taebaek and marries the bear-woman Ungnyeo; Haemosu, son of Heaven, unites with Yuhwa, daughter of the River Earl; Silla's founder emerges from an egg beside a well, heralded by a white horse from the sky. Egg births and heavenly descent tie royal legitimacy to heaven.

## Buddhist names, shamanic gods

The creator figures of the shamanic songs, Mireuk and Seokga, bear the Korean names of the Buddhas Maitreya and Shakyamuni, but in the songs they are rival creator gods whose contest explains why the world is imperfect; they are not Buddhist doctrine. Iryeon, a Buddhist monk, likewise glosses the Lord of Heaven Hwanin as Jeseok, the Buddhist name of Indra. Such layering is typical of Korean religion, in which shamanism, Buddhism, Confucianism, and Daoist elements have long coexisted.

## Living traditions

Korean shamanism remains a living practice, with mudang performing gut for healing, good fortune, and the dead. Dangun is honored on National Foundation Day (Gaecheonjeol, 3 October) in South Korea, whose traditional founding date of 2333 BCE is a calculation by later Joseon-era historians rather than a statement of the Samguk Yusa itself; in North Korea, a 'Mausoleum of Dangun' near Pyongyang, built in 1994 after the reported discovery of his bones, is regarded by most historians outside the country as a political monument rather than an archaeological fact.
